title: Chapter 1. Of Sense
paragraphs: Concerning the thoughts of man, I will consider them first singly, and afterwards in a train, or as they depend upon one another. Taken singly, each one is a representation or appearance of some quality, or other accident, of a body outside us, which is commonly called an Object. This Object works on the eyes, ears, and other parts of a man's body; and by the diversity of its working, it produces a diversity of appearances.

The origin of them all is what we call Sense (for there is no conception in a man's mind that has not, at first, either totally or in parts, been begotten upon the organs of Sense). The rest are derived from that original.

To know the natural cause of Sense is not very necessary to the business now in hand, and I have written about it at length elsewhere. Nevertheless, to fill out each part of my present method, I will briefly state it in this place.

The cause of Sense is the external body, or Object, which presses on the organ proper to each sense, either immediately (as in taste and touch) or mediately (as in seeing, hearing, and smelling). This pressure, through the mediation of nerves and other strings and membranes of the body, is continued inwards to the brain and heart, where it causes a resistance, or counter-pressure, or endeavour of the heart to relieve itself. Because this endeavour is outward, it seems to be some matter outside us. And this seeming, or Fancy, is what men call Sense; consisting, for the eye, in a light or coloured figure; for the ear, in a sound; for the nostril, in an odour; for the tongue and palate, in a savour; and for the rest of the body, in heat, cold, hardness, softness, and other such qualities as we discern by feeling. All these qualities, called sensible, are in the object that causes them merely so many several motions of matter, by which it presses our organs in various ways. And in us who are pressed, they are nothing else but various motions (for motion produces nothing but motion). But their appearance to us is Fancy—the same waking as dreaming. And just as pressing, rubbing, or striking the eye makes us fancy a light, and pressing the ear produces a din, so the bodies we see or hear also produce the same effects by their strong though unobserved action. For if those colours and sounds were in the bodies or objects that cause them, they could not be separated from them, as we see by glasses, and in echoes by reflection, that they are: we know that the thing we see is in one place and its appearance in another. And though at some certain distance the real and very object seems clothed with the fancy it begets in us, still the object is one thing and the image or fancy is another. So that Sense, in all cases, is nothing else but original fancy, caused (as I have said) by the pressure—that is, by the motion—of external things upon our eyes, ears, and other organs ordained for that purpose.

But the philosophy-schools, throughout all the universities of Christendom, grounded on certain texts of Aristotle, teach a different doctrine. They say that the cause of vision is that the thing seen sends out on every side a Visible Species (in English, a Visible Show, Apparition, or Aspect, or a Being Seen); and that the receiving of this into the eye is seeing. As for the cause of hearing, they say the thing heard sends out an Audible Species—that is, an Audible Aspect, or Audible Being Seen—which, entering the ear, produces hearing. And as for the cause of understanding, they also say that the thing understood sends out Intelligible Species, that is, an Intelligible Being Seen, which, coming into the understanding, makes us understand. I do not say this as if I disapproved of the use of universities; but because I shall have to speak hereafter of their office in a Commonwealth, I must let you see on every occasion in passing what things in them stand in need of amendment—among which the frequency of meaningless speech is one.
